claim: Releasing pressure points and tightness in your muscles is so crucial for feeling good, performing and, more importantly, avoiding injury
Injury sucks: training that leads to injury leaves you worse off than not training
One of the most important personal keys to fitness: training in a sustainable, long-term way

Of training in a sustainable, long-term way, maybe the most important part is listening to your body: getting rid of tightness and pressure points, taking an active role in recovery instead of waiting while things build up
Rolling out, the favorite term: the foam roll has its place, but a couple of other tools seem a lot better and more versatile
Staying on top of tightness and sore spots, you feel better and stronger and have longer, harder workouts
Tight muscles after a workout tend to mean worse sleep, maybe for you too
Tightness, a lot of times the kind we can't even really notice until we roll out, builds up until all of a sudden something gets really sore or injured
The aim is to roll out at least a little every day

Probably 15 different foam rolls, massage rollers, sticks and recovery tools were tried over the years, plus plenty of professional massages, and some have their place. The Roll Recovery, spring loaded with lacrosse wheels on both sides, is really awesome, but about 140 bucks and really only has sort of applications to kind of the big parts of your body. The favorite is the most basic and the very cheapest: the Gaiam Restore Pressure Point Massager, from the yoga wellness company, seven bucks on Amazon, probably 15 when bought, "the best seven bucks you've ever spent", used until a couple wore out. Keeping only it, without even professional massage, would be alright. Highly recommended, though any roller you have is a start
The three spiky balls of the Gaiam Restore Pressure Point Massager make it kind of a combination of acupuncture and the release of rolling
A personal favorite thing about the Gaiam Restore Pressure Point Massager: it really helps you notice what is tight
Be proactive, the most important thing found with rollers, stretching and any recovery: wait until something's sore and it's too late
As they say, if you wait until you're thirsty to drink, you're already dehydrated; in recovery, a pain signal means the area has gone beyond tight to really inflamed and hurting
Rolling over your main areas lets you find tight spots and address them before they get painful during activity

Rolling out: quick passes over the entire body, neck down through arms and legs, then working a little more into a sore, really tight spot with a pressure point, or using one of a couple of other favorite rollers
Instead of the pressure point massager, or in addition, use a foam roll, another roller or a professional massage
Recovery is so critical for keeping your body in the game long term, even if you're not training hard
So often, as people age, areas start to hurt, which seemingly largely doesn't have to happen: it's largely built-up tension and tightness, worse over time unaddressed
Before climbing that day, a good 20 minutes of rolling out everywhere loosened things up for a much, much better workout; some versions take two minutes or less of quick passes

The acupuncture kind of action of the pressure point massager's spiky balls really increases blood flow wherever you use it: perfect as a pre-workout warm-up, and great after, for loosening up and digging into sore spots
A promise: rolling out, you will feel the benefits in your body, and really in your mind too
Tight hamstrings, quads and legs especially lead to sort of an uneasiness, and uneasiness in the body translates to the mind
The more relaxed our body, the more relaxed our mind, and the other way too
We hopefully relax the mind with meditation, exercise and enough sleep; releasing tightness feeds the relaxation loop back from the body, for feeling better physically and mentally
